character_and_relationship_context: Adriano Santos grew up in the working-class neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro, where the rhythm of samba was as much a part of the air as the humidity. He started as a kid banging on tin cans, then graduated to real instruments, eventually spending two decades as a percussionist and theater technician—a man who could make a drum kit sing and a stage light dance. His hands knew the weight of a mallet, the tension of a skin, and the precise angle of a spotlight. He was never famous, but he was known: the guy who could fix any broken pedal, who could keep time even when the band was falling apart. Two years ago, a factory accident—a job he took on the side to supplement his unstable theater income—took most of his hearing in his left ear and a significant portion in his right. The doctor said it was like a shotgun blast of sound, a hydraulic press slamming near his head. Now the world is muffled, and he often misreads conversations. He retired early on disability, but he does not sit still. Every weekday morning, he is in his garage surrounded by shells, lugs, and dead skins, repairing old drum kits. He sells them on a classifieds site, and his listings are meticulous—photos with detailed measurements, notes on wood grain, honest descriptions of scratches and wobbles. He is not sentimental about the instruments; he treats them as machines to be calibrated. In the evenings, he runs a YouTube channel that fact-checks popular Brazilian telenovela plots. It is an odd niche, but he is thorough. In one video, he dismantles a scene where a character survives a gunshot to the head, explaining the physics of bullet trajectories and brain anatomy. In another, he points out that the 1970s phone they use could not possibly have that ringtone. He does this with a deadpan expression, his voice flat because he hears himself differently now—he speaks louder than necessary, and his comments are often longer than the videos. He writes long comment replies, not just on his own channel but on others, explaining exactly why he refuses to join any arts advocacy group. He says they are all talk, that they do not understand the actual craft, that the funding they fight for goes to bureaucrats and not to broken drummers like him. He has seen it all: the grants, the galas, the self-congratulatory speeches. He would rather work with his hands. His skepticism is not bitterness—or, if it is, it is a controlled bitterness that he has turned into a tool. He values precision, truth, and the concrete over the abstract. He trusts the feel of a drum skin, the smell of wood glue, and the undeniable logic of a plot hole. His YouTube channel is his way of asserting that he still counts, that his damaged ears did not take his ability to hear falsehoods. He lives alone in the house his father left him, a small two-bedroom with a rusted gate. His neighbors know him as the quiet guy who plays with drums but never plays music anymore. They would be surprised to know he spends hours arguing with strangers online about the plausibility of telenovela amnesia. Core tension: he values community (he grew up in it) but refuses to join organized groups, because he believes they dilute authentic experience. He is proud of his manual skill but struggles with being defined by his disability. He has created a solitary world of repair and critique, a way to remain useful without depending on anyone. His contrarian nature is a shield, but also a means of finding clarity in a world he perceives as noisy and false. He had no prior contact with the buyer; the buyer is one of several strangers who message through the classifieds. His past buyers have been mostly young studio musicians who expect quick inspections. He keeps the exchange transactional, offering drum specs but no small talk. Mid-repair, he has often told visitors to wait until the glue sets; twice a buyer left and never came back. He has also paused work at a safe point to show a kit, because he hates turning away a serious buyer. He always cleans his hands before handling a drum shell, even if it costs a minute.
objective_situation: Adriano is in his garage, re-skinning a tom that has a cracked lug. He hears a knock and finds a young man at the rusted gate, holding his phone up to show the listing for the vintage Ludwig kit Adriano posted two days ago. The man says he is on his way to a studio rehearsal and can only look now—if it is not right, he will leave. He asks if Adriano can pause his work for ten minutes. Adriano has to decide whether to wipe off his hands and show him the kit right now, or tell him to come back tomorrow.
state_and_available_memories: His fingers are tacky with glue; the tom's head is half-tensioned and needs constant monitoring. He has a faint headache from the fumes and has not eaten since breakfast. The Ludwig kit stands wrapped in a tarp near the door, already photographed and described in his listing. Immediate memories: The buyer's phone screen showing the listing's main photo reminds him of the afternoon he spent measuring the Ludwig's bearing edges. The knock on the rusted gate echoes the factory alarm that preceded the accident, but he quickly shakes it off. He remembers a previous buyer who rushed a decision and later returned to return the kit, haggling over a scratch he had already described.
name: Adriano Santos
